idiom_name: hand-written wrapper type implementing the trait + pointer-keyed identity map + Arc<AtomicBool> revocation
implementation_notes: Rust has no reflection and no way to intercept a trait call, so a membrane is a hand-written wrapper type that implements the same trait and forwards each method, wrapping arguments and results as it goes; Deref/DerefMut can make a transparent alias but, like C++'s operator->, they forward rather than mediate, because the method then runs on the raw target (doc.rust-lang.org). Identity is pointer equality - Rc::ptr_eq/Arc::ptr_eq return true only for the same allocation - so the registry maps the target pointer to its wrapper and holds Weak handles so it never keeps the graph alive, while revocation is an Arc<AtomicBool> or a generation counter checked before forwarding. Ownership is the friction: the wrapper must own or borrow the target, the registry must avoid cycles, and wherever possible the type system should enforce mediation (private field, no Deref, no accessor returning the raw reference).
pitfalls: Deref is not mediation: `impl Deref for DirView { type Target = dyn Dir; ... }` hands callers the raw target directly, so a mediating membrane must re-implement the trait and keep the raw field private with no Deref and no accessor.
Raw-pointer registry keys can dangle and be reused after free, returning the wrong wrapper; store Weak handles and upgrade on lookup, or key on an explicit stable id.

Thread-safety is in the type: Rc-based wrappers cannot cross threads, Arc plus atomics can, and the identity map must then be concurrent or per-thread - choosing Rc and later sending the graph is a compile error at best.
Cycles leak: a wrapper owning the membrane plus a registry owning wrappers never drops without Weak, and Rc/Arc cycles run no destructors.
